canonical_statement: The story is set in the sea kingdom of the Sea King, whose castle stands in the deepest part of the ocean, built with walls of coral, long gothic windows of clear amber, and a roof formed of shells that open and close as the water flows over them, each holding a pearl.
context_note: The setting, established in the opening paragraph.

evidence.excerpt: In the deepest spot of all, stands the castle of the Sea King.

Its walls are built of coral, and the long, gothic windows are of
the clearest amber.

The roof is formed of shells, that open and
close as the water flows over them.

canonical_statement: Rank among the merpeople is marked by the number of oysters worn on the tail: the Sea King's mother wears twelve on account of her high birth, while others also of high rank are allowed only six.
context_note: A stated rule of the world with a specific quantity attached -- the kind of detail a reader can check a later scene against.

evidence.excerpt:
she wore twelve
oysters on her tail; while others, also of high rank, were only
allowed to wear six

She was a very wise woman, and
exceedingly proud of her high birth

canonical_statement: The Sea King is a widower whose aged mother keeps house for him and cares for his six grand-daughters, the sea-princesses. The youngest is the prettiest of them, and like all the others she has no feet: her body ends in a fish's tail.
context_note: Who the family is. The tail is stated here because the whole plot turns on exchanging it.

evidence.excerpt:
The Sea King had been a widower for many years, and his aged
mother kept house for him.

They were six beautiful children; but the youngest
was the prettiest of them all

but, like all
the others, she had no feet, and her body ended in a fish's tail

canonical_statement: A mermaid is permitted to rise to the surface of the sea only on reaching her fifteenth year, at which point she may sit on the rocks in the moonlight and see ships, forests and towns. Because each of the six sisters is a year younger than the last, the youngest must wait five years longer than the eldest for her turn.
context_note: The first stated rule of the world, and the one that structures the opening third of the story.

evidence.excerpt:
"When you have reached your fifteenth year," said the
grand-mother, "you will have permission to rise up out of the sea,
to sit on the rocks in the moonlight, while the great ships are
sailing by; and then you will see both forests and towns."

the youngest would have to
wait five years before her turn came to rise up from the bottom of the
ocean, and see the earth as we do

canonical_statement: The youngest princess is quiet and thoughtful, and unlike her sisters -- who delight in objects salvaged from shipwrecks -- she cares for nothing but her red flowers and a beautiful marble statue of a handsome boy, carved from white stone, that fell to the sea floor from a wreck.
context_note: Her character, and the statue -- which the story later uses as the measure of her attachment to the prince.

evidence.excerpt:
She was a strange child, quiet and thoughtful; and while her
sisters would be delighted with the wonderful things which they
obtained from the wrecks of vessels, she cared for nothing but her
pretty red flowers, like the sun, excepting a beautiful marble statue.

It was the representation of a handsome boy, carved out of pure
white stone, which had fallen to the bottom of the sea from a wreck.

canonical_statement: On her own fifteenth birthday the little mermaid rises to the surface and sees a large three-masted ship where a young prince of sixteen is celebrating his birthday with music, lanterns and fireworks.
context_note: The first sight of the prince, and the event that sets the rest of the story going.

evidence.excerpt:
Among
them was a young prince, the most beautiful of all, with large black
eyes; he was sixteen years of age, and his birthday was being kept
with much rejoicing.

A large ship, with three masts, lay becalmed on
the water, with only one sail set

canonical_statement: A storm wrecks the ship. The little mermaid, remembering that human beings cannot live in the water, realizes the prince will die if he sinks, and saves him: she reaches him as he is losing the power of swimming, holds his head above the water, and lets the waves carry them.
context_note: The rescue. Everything that follows depends on it having happened and on nobody else knowing it did.

evidence.excerpt:
she
remembered that human beings could not live in the water, so that when
he got down to her father's palace he would be quite dead. But he must
not die.

She held his head above the water, and let the waves drift
them where they would.

till at length she managed to reach the
young prince, who was fast losing the power of swimming in that stormy
sea

canonical_statement: She carries the prince to a beach near a large white building, lays him in the sunshine with his head raised above his body, and then hides among the rocks with her face covered in sea-foam to watch what becomes of him.
context_note: The decision to hide is the hinge of the plot: it is why the rescue is later misattributed.

evidence.excerpt:
so she swam with the handsome prince to the beach,
which was covered with fine, white sand, and there she laid him in the
warm sunshine, taking care to raise his head higher than his body

then she covered her head and neck with the
foam of the sea so that her little face might not be seen, and watched
to see what would become of the poor prince

canonical_statement: A young girl from the building finds the prince and fetches help, and he revives. Because the little mermaid stayed hidden, he never learns that she saved him -- he sends her no smile, and she returns to her father's castle unhappy.
context_note: The misattribution, established here and paid off at the end when the prince marries the girl he believes rescued him.

evidence.excerpt:
She did not wait long
before she saw a young girl approach the spot where he lay.

But to her he sent
no smile; he knew not that she had saved him.

then she fetched a
number of people, and the mermaid saw that the prince came to life
again, and smiled upon those who stood round him

canonical_statement: The grandmother states the terms of a mermaid's existence: merpeople sometimes live to three hundred years, but when they cease to exist they become only foam on the surface of the water, with not even a grave for those they love. They have no immortal souls and will never live again -- like sea-weed, once cut off they can never flourish more.
context_note: The central rule of the story's world, stated as fact by the character who knows it. Everything the little mermaid does afterwards is an attempt to escape this clause.

evidence.excerpt:
We sometimes live to three
hundred years, but when we cease to exist here we only become the foam
on the surface of the water, and we have not even a grave down here of
those we love.

We have not immortal souls, we shall never live
again; but, like the green sea-weed, when once it has been cut off, we
can never flourish more.

canonical_statement: Human beings, by contrast, have a shorter term of life than merpeople but possess a soul that lives forever, living on after the body has turned to dust and rising up beyond the stars to regions merpeople will never see.
context_note: The other half of the rule. The trade the story turns on is a long life without a soul for a short life with one.

evidence.excerpt:
Human beings, on the contrary, have a soul
which lives forever, lives after the body has been turned to dust.

they must also die, and their term
of life is even shorter than ours

so do they rise to unknown and glorious regions which we shall never
see

canonical_statement: There is exactly one way a mermaid can obtain an immortal soul, and the grandmother states its conditions in full: a man must love her so much that she is more to him than his father and mother, all his thoughts and love must be fixed on her, and a priest must place his right hand in hers while he promises to be true to her here and hereafter. Then his soul glides into her body and she gains a share in the future happiness of mankind -- and he keeps his own soul as well.
context_note: The precise conditions, which the plot then tests one by one and fails on the last. The grandmother's own verdict -- that it can never happen -- is part of the rule.

evidence.excerpt:
unless a man were to love you so much
that you were more to him than his father or mother; and if all his
thoughts and all his love were fixed upon you, and the priest placed
his right hand in yours, and he promised to be true to you here and
hereafter, then his soul would glide into your body and you would
obtain a share in the future happiness of mankind

He would give a
soul to you and retain his own as well; but this can never happen.

canonical_statement: The obstacle the grandmother names is anatomical and cultural: a fish's tail, considered beautiful among merpeople, is thought ugly on earth, where people believe two stout props called legs are necessary in order to be handsome.
context_note: Why the soul is out of reach, stated as a problem with a specific shape -- which is what makes the witch's bargain the obvious next move.

evidence.excerpt:
Your fish's tail, which amongst us is considered so beautiful, is
thought on earth to be quite ugly; they do not know any better, and
they think it necessary to have two stout props, which they call legs,
in order to be handsome.

canonical_statement: The little mermaid states her own valuation explicitly: she would gladly give all the hundreds of years she has to live to be a human being for a single day, for the hope of knowing the happiness of the world above the stars.
context_note: Her motive, stated by her in the terms of an exchange rather than as romance. The prince is the means; the soul is the end.

evidence.excerpt:
I would give gladly all the hundreds of years that I have
to live, to be a human being only for one day, and to have the hope of
knowing the happiness of that glorious world above the stars

"Why have not we an immortal soul?" asked the little mermaid
mournfully

canonical_statement: The sea witch lives beyond a barrier of crushing whirlpools and a warm bubbling mire she calls her turfmoor, in a house built with the bones of shipwrecked human beings, in a forest of polypi -- half animals and half plants -- that seize and hold everything within reach, including the skeletons of drowned people and a strangled mermaid.
context_note: What the journey costs before any bargain is struck, and the first warning the story gives about the witch.

evidence.excerpt:
In the midst of this spot stood a house, built
with the bones of shipwrecked human beings.

Beyond this stood her
house, in the centre of a strange forest, in which all the trees and
flowers were polypi, half animals and half plants

even a little mermaid, whom they had caught
and strangled; and this seemed the most shocking of all to the
little princess

canonical_statement: The witch's draught turns a mermaid's tail into legs, and its stated effects are exact: it must be drunk on shore before sunrise; the transformation feels as if a sword were passing through her; she keeps her floating gracefulness so that no dancer will tread more lightly; and at every step she takes it will feel as if she were treading on sharp knives, and the blood must flow.
context_note: The terms of the transformation, given in advance and in full. The story is careful that nothing about the price is hidden from her.

evidence.excerpt:
Your tail will then disappear, and shrink up
into what mankind calls legs, and you will feel great pain, as if a
sword were passing through you.

you must swim to land tomorrow before sunrise, and sit down on the
shore and drink it

but at every step you take it will feel as if
you were treading upon sharp knives, and that the blood must flow

You will still
have the same floating gracefulness of movement, and no dancer will
ever tread so lightly

canonical_statement: The bargain is irreversible and conditional, and the witch states both parts before the mermaid accepts. Once her shape becomes human she can never be a mermaid again and can never return to her sisters or her father's palace. And if she does not win the prince's love -- so that he is willing to forget his father and mother for her sake, love her with his whole soul, and let a priest join their hands in marriage -- she will never have an immortal soul, and on the first morning after he marries another her heart will break and she will become foam on the crest of the waves.
context_note: The contract's failure clause, stated in advance. It is what makes the ending inevitable rather than cruel.

evidence.excerpt:
for when once your shape has
become like a human being, you can no more be a mermaid

The first morning after he marries another your heart
will break, and you will become foam on the crest of the waves.

You will
never return through the water to your sisters, or to your father's
palace again

and if you do not win the love of the prince, so that he
is willing to forget his father and mother for your sake, and to
love you with his whole soul, and allow the priest to join your
hands that you may be man and wife, then you will never have an
immortal soul

canonical_statement: The witch's price is the little mermaid's voice, which she takes by cutting out her tongue, leaving her permanently dumb and unable ever to speak or sing again. The witch demands it precisely because it is the best thing the mermaid possesses and the thing she was counting on to charm the prince.
context_note: The payment, and the reason the exchange is structured so that the price removes the means of paying the debt.

evidence.excerpt:
You have the sweetest voice of any who dwell here in the
depths of the sea, and you believe that you will be able to charm
the prince with it also, but this voice you must give to me; the
best thing you possess will I have for the price of my draught.

Then she cut off the mermaid's tongue, so that she
became dumb, and would never again speak or sing.

Put out your little tongue that I may cut it
off as my payment; then you shall have the powerful draught.

canonical_statement: The witch's answer to the mermaid's objection that she will have nothing left is that her beautiful form, her graceful walk and her expressive eyes remain, and that with these she can enchain a man's heart.
context_note: The exchange stated as a bet: appearance against speech. The story later resolves the bet against her.

evidence.excerpt:
Your beautiful form, your graceful walk, and your expressive
eyes; surely with these you can enchain a man's heart.

"But if you take away my voice," said the little mermaid, "what is
left for me?"

canonical_statement: The witch does not conceal her judgment of the bargain. She tells the mermaid at the outset that it is very stupid of her, that she shall have her way, and that it will bring her to sorrow.
context_note: The warning, given by the antagonist. The story's rules are never hidden from the character who chooses to break them.

evidence.excerpt:
I know what you want," said the sea witch; "it is very stupid
of you, but you shall have your way, and it will bring you to
sorrow, my pretty princess.

canonical_statement: After drinking the draught before the prince's palace the little mermaid loses consciousness, wakes to find her tail replaced by legs, and is found by the prince with no clothes, so she wraps herself in her long hair. She cannot answer when he asks who she is and where she comes from.
context_note: The transformation and, immediately, the first cost of the price she paid: she cannot answer the one question that would identify her as his rescuer.

evidence.excerpt:
Then the little mermaid drank the magic draught, and it seemed as if a
two-edged sword went through her delicate body: she fell into a swoon,
and lay like one dead.

became aware that her
fish's tail was gone, and that she had as pretty a pair of white
legs and tiny feet as any little maiden could have; but she had no
clothes, so she wrapped herself in her long, thick hair

The prince
asked her who she was, and where she came from, and she looked at
him mildly and sorrowfully with her deep blue eyes; but she could
not speak.

canonical_statement: Every step the little mermaid takes among humans is as the witch said it would be -- as if she were treading on the points of needles or sharp knives -- and she bears it willingly, dancing before the court and climbing mountains with the prince until her feet bleed and her steps are marked, laughing while she does it.
context_note: The ongoing cost, paid continuously and invisibly. The story keeps returning to it precisely because nobody in the palace can see it.

evidence.excerpt:
Every step she took was as the witch had said it would
be, she felt as if treading upon the points of needles or sharp
knives; but she bore it willingly

although her tender feet bled so that even her
steps were marked, she only laughed, and followed him till they
could see the clouds beneath them

though each time
her foot touched the floor it seemed as if she trod on sharp knives

canonical_statement: The prince's affection stops short of the one thing the bargain requires. He loves her as he would love a little child, says she should remain with him always, and gives her a velvet cushion outside his door and a page's dress -- but it never comes into his head to make her his wife, and unless he marries her she cannot receive an immortal soul.
context_note: The precise shape of the failure: affection without marriage, which under the stated rules is worth nothing.

evidence.excerpt:
As the days passed, she loved the prince more fondly, and he loved
her as he would love a little child, but it never came into his head
to make her his wife

yet, unless he married her, she could not
receive an immortal soul; and, on the morning after his marriage
with another, she would dissolve into the foam of the sea

The prince said she should remain with him always, and she
received permission to sleep at his door, on a velvet cushion.

canonical_statement: The prince tells the little mermaid directly why he cannot love her as she needs: he was shipwrecked and cast ashore near a holy temple, and the youngest of the maidens who served there found him and saved his life. He saw her twice, she is the only one in the world he could love, and the little mermaid resembles her closely enough to have almost driven her image from his mind.
context_note: The misattribution stated aloud by the prince, to the one person who could correct it and cannot speak.

evidence.excerpt:
I was in a ship
that was wrecked, and the waves cast me ashore near a holy temple,
where several young maidens performed the service. The youngest of
them found me on the shore, and saved my life.

I saw her but twice,
and she is the only one in the world whom I could love; but you are
like her, and you have almost driven her image out of my mind.

canonical_statement: The little mermaid knows the truth and cannot tell it: she carried the prince over the sea to the wood where the temple stands, sat beneath the foam and watched until human beings came to help him. Because she has no voice, she can only resolve to stay by him, take care of him and give up her life for his sake.
context_note: The story's central irony stated in one place: she holds the fact that would win her everything and has sold the means of saying it.

evidence.excerpt:
"Ah, he knows not that it was I who saved his life," thought the
little mermaid. "I carried him over the sea to the wood where the
temple stands: I sat beneath the foam, and watched till the human
beings came to help him.

I will take
care of him, and love him, and give up my life for his sake.

and the mermaid sighed deeply, but she could
not shed tears

canonical_statement: The prince's marriage is arranged with the daughter of a neighboring king. He tells the little mermaid he cannot love the princess and that if forced to choose a bride he would rather choose her, his dumb foundling with the expressive eyes.
context_note: A near-miss stated explicitly, which sharpens rather than softens the outcome.

evidence.excerpt:
I cannot love her; she is not like the beautiful
maiden in the temple, whom you resemble. If I were forced to choose
a bride, I would rather choose you, my dumb foundling, with those
expressive eyes.

Very soon it was said that the prince must marry, and that the
beautiful daughter of a neighboring king would be his wife, for a fine
ship was being fitted out.

canonical_statement: The neighboring king's daughter turns out to be the temple maiden who found the prince on the shore. He recognizes her as the one who saved his life, embraces her as his bride, and tells the little mermaid that his fondest hopes are all fulfilled and that she will rejoice at his happiness.
context_note: The misattribution completed: the wrong woman is thanked for the rescue in front of the right one, who cannot object.

evidence.excerpt:
"It was you," said the prince, "who saved my life when I lay
dead on the beach," and he folded his blushing bride in his arms.

"Oh,
I am too happy," said he to the little mermaid; "my fondest hopes
are all fulfilled. You will rejoice at my happiness; for your devotion
to me is great and sincere."

People said that she was
being brought up and educated in a religious house, where she was
learning every royal virtue.

canonical_statement: The sisters cut off their hair and give it to the witch in exchange for a way to save the little mermaid: a knife she must plunge into the prince's heart before sunrise. When his warm blood falls on her feet they will grow together into a fish's tail, she will be a mermaid again, and she will return to live out her three hundred years before becoming salt sea foam.
context_note: The escape clause, with its own price and its own exact mechanism. The bargain is reversible after all, but only at the cost the story will not let her pay.

evidence.excerpt:
"We have given our hair to the witch," said they, "to obtain
help for you, that you may not die to-night. She has given us a knife:
here it is, see it is very sharp.

Before the sun rises you must plunge
it into the heart of the prince; when the warm blood falls upon your
feet they will grow together again, and form into a fish's tail, and
you will be once more a mermaid

return to us to live out your
three hundred years before you die and change into the salt sea
foam

canonical_statement: The choice is stated as an exclusive alternative with a deadline: he or she must die before sunrise.
context_note: The story's decision point, reduced by the sisters to a single sentence.

evidence.excerpt: Haste, then; he or you must die before sunrise.
In a few minutes the sun will rise, and you must die.

canonical_statement: The little mermaid does not use the knife. She draws back the curtain, sees the bride resting on the prince's breast, kisses his brow, and when he whispers his bride's name in his sleep she flings the knife far out into the waves and throws herself from the ship into the sea, believing her body is dissolving into foam.
context_note: The refusal, which is the story's moral event: she pays the failure clause rather than escape it at his expense.

evidence.excerpt:
then she flung
it far away from her into the waves; the water turned red where it
fell, and the drops that spurted up looked like blood

She was in his thoughts, and
the knife trembled in the hand of the little mermaid

and then threw
herself from the ship into the sea, and thought her body was
dissolving into foam

canonical_statement: The little mermaid does not dissolve. She finds herself among the daughters of the air, transparent beings whose speech is too ethereal for mortal ears and who are unseen by mortal eyes, and she perceives that she has a body like theirs and is rising higher out of the foam.
context_note: The outcome the stated rules did not provide for -- and the reason the story adds a third rule system to explain it.

evidence.excerpt:
The little
mermaid perceived that she had a body like theirs, and that she
continued to rise higher and higher out of the foam.

all around her
floated hundreds of transparent beautiful beings

their speech was melodious, but too ethereal to be heard by
mortal ears, as they were also unseen by mortal eyes

canonical_statement: The daughters of the air operate under a third rule, stated at the end and distinct from both the mermaids' and the humans': they have no immortal soul either, but unlike a mermaid -- whose eternal destiny hangs on the power of another -- they can procure one by their own good deeds. They fly to warm countries to cool the air that spreads pestilence and carry the perfume of flowers to spread health, and after striving for three hundred years to do all the good in their power they receive an immortal soul.
context_note: The story's resolution of its own central problem: the same goal, reached by one's own action instead of another's love. It is the moral of the fable, stated as a rule.

evidence.excerpt:
But the daughters of the air, although they do not possess an
immortal soul, can, by their good deeds, procure one for themselves.

A mermaid
has not an immortal soul, nor can she obtain one unless she wins the
love of a human being. On the power of another hangs her eternal
destiny.

After we have striven for three hundred
years to all the good in our power, we receive an immortal soul and
take part in the happiness of mankind.

canonical_statement: The little mermaid is admitted to that path on the grounds of what she has already done: she tried with her whole heart to do as the daughters of the air do, suffered and endured, and raised herself to the spirit-world by her good deeds -- so by striving three hundred years in the same way she may obtain an immortal soul.
context_note: The judgment on her conduct, delivered explicitly. The story does not leave the reader to infer whether the sacrifice counted.

evidence.excerpt:
You, poor little mermaid,
have tried with your whole heart to do as we are doing; you have
suffered and endured and raised yourself to the spirit-world by your
good deeds

and now, by striving for three hundred years in the same
way, you may obtain an immortal soul

canonical_statement: The three-hundred-year term is not fixed: it can be shortened or lengthened by the behaviour of children. For every day the daughters of the air find a good child who is the joy of its parents, their time of probation is shortened by a year; for every naughty or wicked child they see, they weep, and every tear adds a day to their trial.
context_note: The closing rule, and the only one addressed past the story to the reader. It is the point at which the fable turns into instruction.

evidence.excerpt:
But when we see a naughty or
a wicked child, we shed tears of sorrow, and for every tear a day is
added to our time of trial!

we can count
one year less of our three hundred years

canonical_statement: The mermaid's final act before rising is to remain unseen: she kisses the forehead of the bride and fans the prince, then mounts with the other children of the air to a rosy cloud, while on the ship the prince and his bride search sorrowfully for her and gaze at the foam as if they knew she had thrown herself into the waves.
context_note: The last image, and the one that closes the concealment motif: she is unseen at the rescue, unseen at the end.

evidence.excerpt:
Unseen she kissed the forehead of her bride, and
fanned the prince, and then mounted with the other children of the air
to a rosy cloud that floated through the aether.

she saw
him and his beautiful bride searching for her; sorrowfully they
gazed at the pearly foam, as if they knew she had thrown herself
into the waves

canonical_statement: The little mermaid weeps for the first time only after she is among the daughters of the air, lifting her glorified eyes towards the sun and feeling them fill with tears -- having earlier been unable to shed tears at all as a mermaid.
context_note: A detail the story sets up early and pays off at the end: tears mark the boundary between what she was and what she has become.

evidence.excerpt:
The little mermaid lifted her glorified eyes towards the sun,
and felt them, for the first time, filling with tears.

and the mermaid sighed deeply, but she could
not shed tears

canonical_statement: Each of the five elder sisters surfaces in turn on her fifteenth birthday and names a different thing as the most beautiful -- a lighted town and its church bells, a sunset with wild swans, a river with green hills and human children, the open sea under a sky like a bell of glass, and winter icebergs larger than churches. Once they are grown and may go whenever they please, all five become indifferent to the surface and say it is pleasanter at home.
context_note: The structural device the first pass cut: five satisfied appetites set against one that is not. It is what makes the youngest's longing a difference in kind rather than in degree.

evidence.excerpt:
As soon as the eldest was fifteen, she was allowed to rise to
the surface of the ocean.

When first the sisters had permission to rise to the surface, they
were each delighted with the new and beautiful sights they saw; but
now, as grown-up girls, they could go when they pleased, and they
had become indifferent about it.

In another year the second sister received permission to rise to
the surface of the water, and to swim about where she pleased.

large icebergs were
floating about, each like a pearl, she said, but larger and loftier
than the churches built by men

canonical_statement: Mermaids have no tears, and the story states that they therefore suffer more. The little mermaid stands alone watching her sisters rise arm-in-arm, ready to cry and unable to.
context_note: Established early and paid off in the final scene, where she weeps for the first time only after ceasing to be a mermaid. Without it the ending's tears are decoration.

evidence.excerpt:
ready to cry, only that the mermaids have no tears, and
therefore they suffer more

When the sisters rose, arm-in-arm, through the water in this
way, their youngest sister would stand quite alone, looking after
them

canonical_statement: Rank is paid for in pain. When the little mermaid turns fifteen her grandmother orders eight great oysters to attach themselves to her tail to show her high rank, and when she says they hurt, the answer is that pride must suffer pain.
context_note: The story's first statement of its own economics -- that status costs pain -- offered before the bargain in which she accepts far more of it for far more.

evidence.excerpt: "Pride must suffer pain," replied the old lady.

Then
the old lady ordered eight great oysters to attach themselves to the
tail of the princess to show her high rank.
"But they hurt me so," said the little mermaid.

canonical_statement: The little mermaid's voice is established as the finest anywhere before the witch demands it: merpeople have lovelier voices than anyone on earth, she sings more sweetly than all of them, and the whole court applauds her with hands and tails at the ball she leaves in order to seek the witch.
context_note: The valuation that makes the witch's price checkable rather than asserted. It is stated in the scene immediately before she goes to sell it.

evidence.excerpt:
No one on earth has such a lovely voice as theirs.
The little mermaid sang more sweetly than them all.

The whole court
applauded her with hands and tails

for she knew she had the loveliest voice of any on earth or
in the sea

canonical_statement: After the transformation the sisters come to the surface every night, and once the grandmother -- who had not surfaced for many years -- and the Sea King himself appear, wearing his crown. They stretch out their hands towards her but do not venture as near the land as the sisters do.
context_note: The only evidence of what her family does after she goes, and a qualification on the witch's terms: she cannot return to them, but they can come partway to her.

evidence.excerpt:
and once she saw in the
distance her old grandmother, who had not been to the surface of the
sea for many years, and the old Sea King, her father, with his crown
on his head

They stretched out their hands towards her, but they
did not venture so near the land as her sisters did.

canonical_statement: The witch supplies a defence for the return journey -- a few drops of the potion thrown over the polypi would tear their fingers into a thousand pieces -- but the mermaid has no need of it, because the polypi spring back in terror at the sight of the glittering draught, which shines in her hand like a twinkling star.
context_note: Closes the forest passage, and demonstrates the potion's power before it is drunk.
